organizations.name: United States Preventive Services Task Force

recommendations.title: Statin Use for Primary CVD Prevention
recommendations.recommendation_text: Prescribe a low- to moderate-dose statin for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 75 who have 1 or more CVD risk factors (dyslipidemia, diabetes, hypertension, or smoking) and an estimated 10-year CVD event risk of 10% or greater.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 40–75 with at least one heart disease risk factor (high cholesterol, diabetes, high blood pressure, or smoking) and a 10% or higher 10-year cardiovascular risk should discuss statin therapy with their doctor to prevent a first heart attack or stroke.

recommendations.title: Preeclampsia Prevention: Low-Dose Aspirin
recommendations.recommendation_text: Prescribe low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) as preventive medication after 12 weeks of gestation in persons who are at high risk for preeclampsia. High-risk factors include a prior history of preeclampsia, multifetal pregnancy, chronic hypertension, type 1 or 2 diabetes, kidney disease, or autoimmune conditions.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you are pregnant and at high risk for preeclampsia — due to prior preeclampsia, carrying multiples, chronic high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney disease — your doctor may recommend low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) starting after 12 weeks of pregnancy.

recommendations.title: Aspirin for CVD Primary Prevention — Do Not Initiate (Age 60+)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Do not initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults 60 years or older. The harms of aspirin initiation (major gastrointestinal, intracranial, and extracranial bleeding) outweigh the benefits in this age group.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you are 60 or older and have not had a heart attack or stroke, you should not start taking daily aspirin to prevent one — the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit. If you already take daily aspirin, talk with your doctor before stopping. This does not apply to people prescribed aspirin after a heart attack or stroke.

recommendations.title: Aspirin for CVD Primary Prevention — Individualized Decision (Ages 40–59)
recommendations.recommendation_text: The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year cardiovascular disease risk should be an individual one. Evidence indicates that the net benefit of aspirin use in this group is small. Persons who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you are 40–59 with a 10% or higher 10-year risk of heart disease, starting daily low-dose aspirin is a personal choice to make with your doctor — the benefit is small and must be weighed against bleeding risk. It makes most sense for people at higher heart risk and low bleeding risk.

recommendations.title: Low-Dose Aspirin for CVD and Colorectal Cancer Primary Prevention (Ages 50–59)
recommendations.recommendation_text: Initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and colorectal cancer in adults aged 50 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year cardiovascular disease risk, are not at increased risk for bleeding, have a life expectancy of at least 10 years, and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily for at least 10 years.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: Adults 50–59 with a 10% or higher 10-year heart disease risk, low bleeding risk, and at least a 10-year life expectancy may benefit from daily low-dose aspirin — it reduces the risk of a first heart attack and, over the long term, colorectal cancer. This is an older (2016) recommendation; discuss with your doctor how it fits with the 2022 aspirin guidance.

recommendations.title: Statin Therapy for Adults with Diabetes (Ages 40–75)
recommendations.recommendation_text: For people with diabetes aged 40–75 years without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, use moderate-intensity statin therapy in addition to lifestyle therapy. High-intensity statin therapy is recommended for those at higher cardiovascular risk, including those with one or more ASCVD risk factors.
recommendations.patient_facing_summary: If you have diabetes and are 40–75 years old, you should be on a statin (usually moderate-intensity) even if your cholesterol is not high — statins reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people with diabetes. Your doctor may recommend a stronger statin if your risk is higher.
